copy.official: the Florida Department of Environmental Protection or Florida State Parks
copy.gary: I've been wandering Florida's state parks and I still find something new on most visits, like a cold, clear spring on a hot afternoon or a manatee drifting by in winter.
copy.description: Check in at every Florida state park you visit, from the springs to the Keys, collect stamps and badges, rate your favorites and explore with your Park Pals.
copy.made_for: Florida’s state parks, from the Panhandle to the Keys

motifs.name: Springs
motifs.blurb: Florida has more than a thousand springs, and many of the clearest bubble up in state parks, like Ichetucknee and Wakulla.

motifs.name: Manatees
motifs.blurb: In winter, manatees gather in the warm water of springs such as Blue Spring State Park, where you can watch them from the boardwalk.

motifs.name: The first undersea park
motifs.blurb: John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park in Key Largo was the first undersea park in the United States.

motifs.name: Lighthouses
motifs.blurb: The Cape Florida Lighthouse in Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park, built in 1825, is the oldest standing structure in Miami-Dade County.

motifs.name: Gopher tortoises
motifs.blurb: Gopher tortoise burrows shelter hundreds of other species, from snakes to burrowing owls. Watch for them along sandy trails.

motifs.name: Paynes Prairie
motifs.blurb: Wild horses and bison roam the wide grassland of Paynes Prairie Preserve State Park, just south of Gainesville.

motifs.name: Falling Waters
motifs.blurb: Falling Waters State Park in the Panhandle has Florida’s highest waterfall, tumbling 73 feet into a sinkhole.
